title: The Easter Island ‘heads’ have bodies, many buried up to the shoulders
body: The moai of Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, are whole-body figures carved mostly between 1250 and 1500 from the volcanic tuff of the Rano Raraku quarry. Their heads are huge, about **three-eighths of each statue**, and the best-known photographs show statues on the quarry’s slopes buried to the shoulders, which is how the idea of bodiless heads took hold. Excavated ‘heads’ there turned out to have torsos with carved markings protected by the soil. More than 900 moai are known; hundreds were moved to stone platforms around the coast, where they gazed inland over their clan lands.

slides.alt: Cross-section sketch of a moai: the head and shoulders rise above a ground line while the torso and arms continue below it, with labels ‘above ground’ and ‘buried’.
slides.caption: On the slopes of Rano Raraku, the quarry where most moai were carved, the soil hides the torso. The head alone is about three-eighths of the statue.

slides.heading: A moai’s head is about three-eighths of the whole statue
slides.note: The rest, hidden by soil on the quarry slopes, is a torso with arms but no legs.

slides.label: moai known on Rapa Nui; nearly half are still at the Rano Raraku quarry
slides.text: The tallest ever erected, Paro, stood almost 10 metres tall and weighed 82 tonnes.

left.label: The myth
left.text: Giant heads rest on the ground with nothing beneath them.

right.label: The fact
right.text: Each has a torso and arms but no legs; the famous quarry statues are simply buried to the shoulders.

slides.heading: Did they walk?
slides.text: Island stories say the statues walked. Scholars now favour a version of that: moai were ‘walked’ upright, rocked from side to side with ropes, partly because the deforested island may have lacked timber for sledges and rollers. The debate continues.

slides.question: How much of a moai is its head?
slides.explanation: Heads make up three-eighths of the whole statue. Together with the quarry statues buried to the shoulders, that created the myth of bodiless heads.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: The moai are just giant heads
They have torsos and arms but no legs
They were carved from volcanic tuff
The coastal moai looked out to sea

slides.explanation: The coastal moai faced inland, over their clan lands. Most were cut from the tuff of Rano Raraku, where nearly half of the 900-plus known statues remain.
